frequency_question: How often do structural friction points (such as sub-national state government dissent or federal-state institutional conflict) completely block the signing of a negotiated transboundary water treaty within a short-term window?
membership_rule: Includes formal bilateral water treaty renewals or negotiations involving federal states where sub-national governments hold constitutional or political veto power over implementation.

cases.name: India-Pakistan Indus Waters Treaty Modifications (ongoing friction, no new treaty)
Mekong River Commission Procedures for Notification (signed 2003 despite domestic friction)
Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II Agreement (signed 2011)
Senegal River Basin Development Organisation Charter Revisions (2002)
US-Canada Columbia River Treaty Review (ongoing structural friction, delayed past windows)

coverage_note: 6 named cases covering major federal transboundary water negotiations with sub-national friction.
known_gaps: Excludes minor administrative water-sharing protocols that lack high-level sub-national political friction.
skeleton: Total relevant high-friction transboundary treaty processes identified in federal/multi-tier contexts over 3 successful vs 3 stalled major outcomes.
multiplier: 3 hits out of 6 total comparable structural friction cases yields a baseline rate of 50 percent.
validity_reason: Transboundary hydro-diplomacy norms and federal-state structural friction dynamics evolve slowly over multi-year political cycles.
